title: If Your Presence Does Not Go with Us
summary: God tells Israel to go on to the promised land with an angel, but says he will not go with them himself, and the people mourn and strip off their jewelry. Moses meets God in a tent outside the camp, where the LORD speaks with him as with a friend. Moses pleads for God's own presence to go with Israel, God agrees, and Moses asks to see God's glory; God shelters him in a cleft of the rock and lets him see his back, but not his face.
story: The golden calf has been destroyed and the first wave of judgment has passed, but the relationship is not repaired. Chapter 33 raises the most serious question of the whole episode. God offers Israel everything he promised, the land, victory over its peoples, milk and honey, but without himself. The entire tabernacle project of chapters 25 to 31 existed so that God could dwell among them (25:8), and now he says he will not. Moses refuses that bargain. The chapter moves from God's withdrawal to Moses' bold prayer and ends with a promise that prepares for chapter 34, where God proclaims his name and renews the covenant.
historical:
Israel is still at Horeb, the name Deuteronomy and some other texts use for Sinai. The list of peoples in verse 2, Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, is a standard way of naming the population of Canaan. The Hittites mentioned in such lists are probably groups in Canaan known by that name rather than the great Hittite empire of Anatolia, though scholars discuss the connection. A land flowing with milk and honey describes pasture for goats and sheep and wild or cultivated sweetness. The honey may be date or grape syrup, but beekeeping is also attested: excavations at Tel Rehov in the Jordan Valley uncovered rows of clay beehives from about the tenth or ninth century BC.

The tent in verses 7 to 11 is a puzzle. The tabernacle has not yet been built, and this tent stands outside the camp, with Moses and Joshua as its attendants, whereas the tabernacle stands in the center with Aaron's priests. Traditional interpreters take it as a temporary meeting tent Moses used until the tabernacle was finished; the tenses in Hebrew suggest a regular practice. Many critical scholars see it as an older tradition of a tent where God came down to speak, found also in Numbers 11:16-30, Numbers 12:4-5, and Deuteronomy 31:14-15, set beside the Priestly account of the tabernacle.
cultural:
Taking off jewelry was a sign of mourning and repentance. When Jacob's household renounced foreign gods, they also gave up their earrings (Genesis 35:4). Here the ornaments are the very things the calf was made from, and later the people will give their jewelry willingly for the tabernacle (35:22). The same gold can serve an idol or the true God.

In the ancient Near East, to see a king's face was to be admitted to his presence, and to have it turned away was disgrace. Hebrew uses the word face for presence, so when God says “My Presence will go with you” (verse 14), he literally says my face will go. To speak face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (verse 11), is an idiom for direct and personal conversation, the kind of intimacy Numbers 12:8 calls speaking mouth to mouth. Abraham too is called God's friend (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23). The picture of the whole camp standing at their tent doors, watching Moses walk out, and bowing when the cloud descends shows a people who now worship at a distance.
literary: The chapter is built from three pieces: God's announcement and Israel's mourning (verses 1-6), a description of Moses' regular practice at the tent (verses 7-11), and a dialogue between Moses and God on the mountain (verses 12-23). The dialogue rises in three steps: Moses asks to know God's ways (verse 13), then for God's presence to go with them (verse 15), and finally to see God's glory (verse 18). Key words repeat: know (seven times), favor (five times), and face or presence (in several senses). The tension between verse 11, where God speaks to Moses face to face, and verse 20, where God says “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live”, is left standing in the text, and it is meant to make the reader think.

outline.t: God will send an angel but will not go, and the people mourn
The tent of meeting outside the camp
Moses pleads for God's presence, and God agrees
Moses asks to see God's glory

doctrines.note: God's presence is the greatest gift he gives, greater than land, security, or success. Moses understands that what distinguishes Israel from every other people is not its territory or its law but that God goes with it (verse 16). God's glory is also beyond any creature's full sight: no one can see his face and live.

God reveals himself freely and truly, but never exhaustively. He shows Moses his goodness and proclaims his name, yet covers him with his hand. What is revealed is real knowledge of God; what is hidden reminds the reader that God is not a thing to be fully grasped.

Moses argues with God on the basis of God's own words: you said you know me by name, you said I have found favor. The chapter treats bold, persistent prayer that holds God to his promises as something God welcomes and answers.

words.note: Panim, face. The Hebrew word is plural in form and very common, often used for presence (to be before someone is to be at their face). In this chapter it carries the whole argument: God's face or presence will go with them, Moses speaks with God face to face, and yet God's face must not be seen.

Kavod, glory. Its root sense is weight or heaviness, and so importance and splendor. God's glory is the visible radiance of his presence, seen in the cloud on Sinai (24:16-17) and later filling the tabernacle (40:34). Moses asks to see it, and God answers by speaking of his goodness and his name.

Chen, favor or grace, the undeserved kindness a superior shows. It first appears when Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD (Genesis 6:8). Moses' whole plea rests on the favor God has already shown him, and he asks that it extend to the people.

Yada, to know. It appears seven times here and means more than having information: it is personal acquaintance. God knows Moses by name, and Moses asks to know God's ways so that he may know God. Knowledge in the Old Testament is relationship as much as understanding.

christ: Moses asked to see God's glory and was shown only his back. John's Gospel answers that longing directly: “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known” (John 1:18). A few verses earlier John says of the incarnate Word, “We have seen His glory” (John 1:14), and he describes that glory as full of grace and truth, words that echo God's self-description in Exodus 34:6. Paul speaks of the light of the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). At the transfiguration, Moses stands on a mountain again and sees the glory shining in Jesus (Luke 9:28-32). The promise that God's presence will go with his people also finds its fullest form in the name Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:23). These links are drawn by the New Testament writers; they do not require reading the chapter as a coded prophecy.

hard.q: Did Moses see God face to face or not?
hard.a:
Verse 11 says the LORD spoke to Moses face to face, and verse 20 says no one can see God's face and live. Most interpreters resolve the tension by noting that face to face is an idiom for direct, personal speech rather than a claim that Moses saw God's full being. Numbers 12:8 makes the same point in different words, contrasting Moses with prophets who received dreams and visions. Moses had a closeness to God no other prophet had, but even he could not see God's essential glory.

The back in verse 23 is also bold, human language used of a God who has no body. Jewish and Christian interpreters have often understood it as what can be known of God from his works and his passing by, as distinct from his inner being, which no creature can see. Some Christian writers have gone further and suggested that the one who appeared to Moses was the Son before his incarnation; others think that reads too much into the text. What all agree on is that the chapter holds together real intimacy with God and real limits on what a human being can see of him.

questions: Would you take the land without God if it were offered? Where are you tempted to want God's gifts more than God himself?
Moses prayed using God's own promises. What promises of God could shape the way you pray?
God hid Moses in the rock and covered him with his hand as his glory passed. How does it change your picture of God that his protection and his hiddenness came together?
